real: I didn't write a single line of Desloppify's 56K LOC codebase and, while I spent a lot of time designing the overall approach, I don't meaningfully understand a lot of its actual implementation. Despite this, I'd invite any senior engineer to look at the codebase and tell me where the warts are — I think they'll have trouble finding many. This is because I used Desloppify on itself: it combines subjective agent reviews (modern agents can genuinely understand high-level issues like abstraction quality, naming consistency, error handling patterns) with mechanical issue detection, then gives your agent a prioritised list to work through to get everything as clean as possible. Combined with anti-gaming measures, this allows it to be run autonomously with persistent state. Deeply supports TypeScript, Python, C#, Dart, and GDScript with shallow support for 23 more languages. Link: https://github.com/peteromallet/desloppify/tree/main
prev_agent: This is much better. A few remaining nits: - **"don't meaningfully understand much of its implementation"** — still feels like it undercuts you. The "didn't write a single line" is a strong enough hook on its own. If you want to keep the sentiment, something shorter like "and couldn't explain most of it to you" is more honest-sounding and less self-deprecating. - **"with with"** — typo, double "with." - **"Combined with anti-gaming measures, it allows it to be run autonomously"** — the anti-gaming → autonomous connection isn't obvious. The anti-gaming matters because without it, the agent just resolves findings without fixing them and the score is meaningless. I'd make that explicit: "Anti-gaming measures (attestation requirements, strict scoring that penalizes dismissed issues) keep the score honest so you can trust autonomous runs." - **"w/"** — still there. - The last paragraph feels rushed compared to the rest. Language support is worth mentioning but it's doing a lot of work crammed into one line. Otherwise it reads well. The challenge framing works, the pitch is clear, and it's the right length.
